newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Housing, Q3 GDP data, FOMC meets.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Housing, Q3 GDP data, FOMC meets.

text.p: The market gets a varied lot of new economic data in the coming week and while none of it is likely to be dramatic news, prices could still get pushed around, given current, volatile trading, analysts said.

"There's more downside risk than upside," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "The market's tone is not deeply negative, but I think people are rethinking their investment strategies and interest-rate outlooks. If you were going to see any price move, I would think it would be toward lower prices and higher yields."
The bond market ended higher on Friday after a week of volatile trade. The 30-year bond rose 20/32 to 99 even, its yield at 6.58 percent, versus 6.51 percent at Friday's close a week earlier.
The coming week opens with the Federal Reserve's report on November U.S. industrial production.

Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, a 0.6 percent production rise, constituting a rebound after a 0.5 percent decline in October which economists tied mainly to the effects of a Canadian autoworkers strike against General Motors Corp.
The automaker's plants were all running again by early November, contributing to a production rebound, they said.
Data on capacity use, the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in its production, are released in conjunction with the industrial production figure.
Capacity use is expected to edge up 83.0 percent from 82.7 percent in October, still far below what it would take to generate any inflation pressure, economists said.
November housing starts data are due on Tuesday. They are predicted to have bounced to an annualized 1.39 million units after falling sharply to 1.366 million in October.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy-making arm of the Federal Reserve, also meets on Tuesday, as scheduled. The policy makers are expected to leave interest rates unchanged.

"If you look at the economic statistics, they do not justify a tightening," said Moran. "And if you consider all the developments around the Greenspan 'irrationality' speech, those would also make it very difficult to tighten right now. If they tightened now, they'd see an extreme market reaction, and I don't think they want that."
Weekly jobless claims data, due Thursday, are expected to bounce higher to 331,000 new claims from an unexpectedly low level of 317,000 new claims a week earlier.
Economists view the claims data in the last month of the year with an ounce of skepticism, noting that holidays and bad weather conditions can affect the filing and processing of unemployment claims.

Also on Thursday, the market gets October US trade data. The US trade gap is estimated to have narrowed to $10.4 billion in October from $11.34 billion in September, news that is not likely to directly affect Treasury securities prices.
"I don't see the trade data as having the potential to move the market," said Moran.
The Philadelphia Federal Reserve's survey of area business conditions will draw some attention. The Reuters poll forecast a reading of 7.4 for November, up from 6.4 in October.
The final figures for third-quarter GDP are expected to be left at +2.0 percent, as previously reported.
Federal funds will probably open at 5-3/8 percent on Monday, dealers indicated.
